analysis.one_liner: Expands Social Security benefits and funds them with payroll taxes on income above $400,000.
analysis.headline: Backed by 189 of 216 House Democrats, the bill never received a committee vote and died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would raise Social Security checks across the board, use a cost-of-living formula that better reflects seniors' expenses, raise the minimum benefit for long-time low earners, and restore full benefits to teachers and other public workers whose checks were reduced by the windfall and government pension offsets. It would also end the five-month wait for disability benefits, extend benefits for students up to age 26, and protect Social Security field offices from closing. To pay for it, all wages above $400,000 would become subject to the Social Security payroll tax, and the bill would apply Social Security tax to net investment income.
analysis.who_benefits: Roughly all of the tens of millions of Americans receiving Social Security or disability benefits, and future retirees: bigger monthly checks (a temporary benefit-formula boost), a larger cost-of-living adjustment keyed to senior spending, a minimum benefit at or above the poverty line for people who worked long careers at low wages, caregiver credits for people who left work to care for family, restored benefits for widows and widowers and for public workers hit by the windfall elimination and government pension offsets, no five-month wait for disability checks, and student children of deceased, disabled, or retired workers covered through age 25.

how_it_helps.text: Temporarily raises the benefit formula so that the lowest earnings band counts at 93% instead of 90%, increasing checks for everyone, for 2025 through 2034.

Switches the annual cost-of-living adjustment to whichever index is higher — the standard wage-earner index or the senior-specific CPI for Elderly Consumers — recognizing that retirees spend more on health care.
Sets a new minimum benefit pegged to the federal poverty guideline that scales up with years worked, aimed at people who worked decades at low wages.

Repeals the windfall elimination provision and the government pension offset, which currently cut benefits for about three million public employees and their spouses who also have pensions from jobs not covered by Social Security.

Eliminates the five-month waiting period for disability benefits and replaces the current cliff where benefits are cut off entirely with a gradual $1-off-for-$2 reduction as earnings rise, making it easier to try working again.
Credits up to five years of unpaid family caregiving as if the caregiver had earned wages, so parents and people caring for chronically dependent relatives don't lose retirement benefits.
Bars the Social Security Administration from closing field and hearing offices without public hearings and other conditions, protecting in-person service especially in rural areas.

analysis.who_pays: High earners and investors. Wages and self-employment income above $400,000 — currently exempt from the Social Security payroll tax above a much lower annual cap — would be taxed, and the bill would apply Social Security tax to net investment income. Employers would pay the matching payroll tax on their executives' and high earners' wages above the cap. The bill counts only a small share of that new taxed income in the benefit formula, so top earners would pay substantially more in without a proportional benefit back.

drawbacks.text: Most of the benefit improvements are written as temporary: the across-the-board increase, the senior cost-of-living index, the poverty-level minimum benefit, the widow/widower fix, and the caregiver credits all have effective dates of 2025 through 2034 and would need to be renewed or made permanent by a later Congress.

Earnings above $400,000 are taxed but count in the benefit formula at only a 1% factor, so high earners would pay the full 12.4% payroll tax on that income while receiving almost nothing extra back — a good-faith objection that the bill breaks the link between what people pay in and what they get out.

The new taxes — payroll tax above $400,000 plus a Social Security tax on net investment income — fall on the highest-income households and on the employers of highly paid executives, and any broad tax increase of this kind raises arguments about its effect on work and investment decisions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are broad and concrete: larger checks, a fairer inflation adjustment, a poverty-floor minimum, restored benefits for widows and defrauded-by-formula public workers, and faster disability payments — affecting virtually every beneficiary household. The costs are concentrated and narrow: wages above $400,000 and investment income, which almost no working household reaches. The main design weakness is that most benefit expansions sunset after ten years, so the package is less durable than its framing suggests. On balance this is a large, clearly financed transfer toward ordinary beneficiaries, paid for by those least likely to be harmed by it.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in committee from the day it was introduced and never got a markup or floor vote before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. John Larson of Connecticut introduced the Social Security 2100 Act on July 12, 2023, with 188 original cosponsors including House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries and Majority Whip Jim Clyburn.

It was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and also to the Education and the Workforce and Energy and Commerce Committees; within two days it went to the Health Subcommittee, and in December 2024 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Social Security.
189 House Democrats cosponsored the bill — 87% of the Democratic caucus — but no Republican cosponsored it and no committee ever voted on it.

The bill received no further action of any kind and expired when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, meaning every cosponsor would have had to reintroduce it from scratch in the new Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Households earning above $400,000 and holders of substantial investment income are better off, since they will not pay the new payroll and investment-income taxes. Social Security beneficiaries who would have received larger checks, public workers whose benefits would have been restored, and disability claimants facing the five-month wait are worse off.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners spared the new taxes

for.name: Rep. John Larson (D-CT)
for.role: Sponsor; senior member of the Ways and Means Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Social Security 2100 Act on July 12, 2023, and built a large cosponsor coalition behind it.

for.name: 189 of 216 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including the House Democratic Leader, the Majority Whip, and the top Democrat on Ways and Means.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Primary committee of referral, chaired by a Republican in the 118th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never held a markup or vote on the bill in the 18 months between its introduction and the end of the Congress; the bill's last action was a referral to a subcommittee on December 17, 2024.

against.name: House Republican majority
against.role: Majority party controlling the House calendar and committee chairs
against.what_they_did: No House Republican cosponsored the bill, and the Republican-controlled committees to which it was referred never advanced it to the floor.

sides.party_line_note: All 190 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; not a single House Republican signed on, and the bill died in a Republican-chaired committee without a vote.

industries.industry: Households with wages or investment income above $400,000
industries.note: The bill applies the 12.4% Social Security payroll tax to all wages and self-employment income above $400,000 (currently exempt above a much lower cap) and would apply Social Security tax to net investment income. Their loss funds the benefit increases, and their interest in this bill ran directly against beneficiaries'.

industries.industry: Large employers of highly paid executives
industries.note: Employers pay a matching Social Security payroll tax, so the $400,000 threshold creates a new payroll cost on high earners' wages above the cap for companies paying them.

industries.industry: Public employees with non-covered pensions (teachers, police, state and local workers)
industries.note: Repealing the windfall elimination provision and government pension offset restores Social Security benefits currently reduced for millions of these workers and their widows and widowers.
